label: E4
title: Heat and temperature; how heat moves

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
Temperature is a measure of how hot or cold something is. Heat is the spontaneous transfer of energy due to a temperature difference. Heat is measured in joules, the SI unit of energy. Temperature is measured in degrees Celsius or in kelvin.

The specific heat of a substance is the heat required to change the temperature of one kilogram of it by one degree Celsius. Its unit is joules per kilogram per degree Celsius.

The letter Q stands for the quantity of heat transferred. The letter m stands for the mass of the substance. The letter c stands for its specific heat.

Q = m times c times ΔT

The change in temperature is the final temperature minus the initial temperature.

Every process involving heat transfer takes place by only three methods. Conduction is heat transfer through stationary matter by physical contact. Convection is heat transfer by the macroscopic movement of a fluid. Heat transfer by radiation occurs when microwaves, infrared radiation, visible light, or another form of electromagnetic radiation is emitted or absorbed.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
Temperature is how hot a thing is. A thermometer reads it. It is a level, not an amount. It does not care how much of the thing there is. A spoonful of boiling water and a bucket of boiling water are at the same temperature.

Heat is energy moving, because one thing is hotter than another. It is an amount, and it is measured in joules, like every other energy in this book.

So the bucket and the spoonful are at the same temperature and hold very different amounts of energy.

Energy goes from the hotter thing to the colder thing, and it keeps going until the two are at the same temperature. Then it stops.

The letter Q stands for the quantity of heat. The letter m stands for the mass. The letter c stands for the number belonging to the material. The Greek capital letter delta, written Δ, is how mathematics writes “the change in”. So the pair ΔT stands for the change in temperature, and it is read “delta T”.

Q = m times c times ΔT

That number belonging to the material has a name: the specific heat. It is the joules you need for one kilogram of the stuff to go up by one degree.

material joules for one kilogram, one degree
water 4186
glass 840
iron and steel 452

Water needs more than nine times as much energy as steel for the same rise. A bigger temperature rise does not mean more heat went in. It means the two things were different things.

One more word, because the section on the calorimeter used it without naming it. Heat capacity is the same idea for one particular object rather than for a material. It is the joules that object needs to go up by one degree. A calorimeter has one, and you have already used it. The energy equivalent from that section is the calorimeter’s heat capacity. It is also why a calorimeter’s degrees can be trusted: inside one instrument the object never changes, so the number never changes.

The change in temperature is the temperature at the end minus the temperature at the start. If the thing cooled, that subtraction gives a negative number, and so does Q. It means the energy went out rather than in.

Last, how heat actually gets from one place to another. There are exactly three ways, and that is not a list somebody stopped writing. It is all of them.

Conduction is touching. Energy moves through matter that is staying put, by contact. A steel tumbler of hot chai and your fingers.

Convection is carrying. A fluid — a liquid or a gas — moves, and the energy goes with it. Hot air rising off a tawa. Blood carrying warmth from the middle of you out to your skin.

Radiation is shining. Energy crosses as light, or as the invisible light below red that bodies give off, and it needs nothing in between. The warmth on your face from an open fire across the room.

Anything that keeps something warm or cool acts on one of them directly. So when somebody tells you their product keeps heat in, ask two questions. Which of the three does it act on? And what happens to the other two?

blocks.label: Illustration
blocks.html:
In the calorimeter, a bigger temperature rise meant more energy.

Go and break it, with two things you have in the kitchen.

Take a steel tawa that weighs one kilogram. Take one kilogram of water in a pan. Put them on two identical burners and give each exactly the same amount of energy.

Use 4,186 joules, because it makes the first sum come out at one.

Multiply the mass by the specific heat to get the joules it needs for one degree.

1 times 4186 = 4186

You are giving it exactly that, so the water goes up by one degree Celsius.

Now the steel, the same way.

1 times 452 = 452

So 4,186 joules will take the tawa a long way up.

Divide the energy by what it needs for one degree. That is 4,186 divided by 452, which comes to 9.26 degrees Celsius, to two decimal places. Check it backwards.

452 times 9.26 = 4185.52

That is within half a joule of 4,186.

One thermometer reads a rise of one degree and the other reads a rise of more than nine. The temperature rise did not measure the heat. It measured the heat divided by what the object needed per degree, and the two objects needed very different amounts.

Inside one calorimeter the object never changes. So the joules it needs per degree never change either, and that is the energy equivalent you were handed.

Within one instrument, twice the rise is twice the energy. Across two instruments it is worth nothing, because the two heat capacities differ and nobody has said by how much.

Two hundred grams of chai are poured at 95 degrees Celsius and left. An hour later they are at 30. The change in temperature is the end minus the start.

30 minus 95 = -65

Now the energy, taking 0.2 kilograms of a liquid that is mostly water.

0.2 times 4186 = 837.2
837.2 times -65 = -54418

Minus 54,418 joules. The minus sign says it left.

Pour chai into a steel tumbler and pick it up. Your fingers know within a second. The steel stayed where it was and the energy came through it into your hand. Now pour the same chai into a clay kulhar and pick that up. You can hold it. Nothing about the chai changed. The matter between the chai and your fingers did.

Hold your palm a foot above a hot tawa, not touching it. The air over the tawa is being heated, it rises, and it brings the energy up to your hand.

Stand three feet from an open tandoor and face it. Your face warms, and the air in between did not have to carry anything.

Now the part that makes the three names useful rather than decorative. Read what the same section says about controlling them.

We can control rates of heat transfer by choosing materials (such as thick wool clothing for the winter), controlling air movement (such as the use of weather stripping around doors), or by choice of color (such as a white roof to reflect summer sunlight).

Choosing the material acts on how easily heat gets through it. Stopping the air moving acts on convection. Choosing the colour acts on radiation.

Take a sheet of paper and write the three routes down the left side. Then put the claim against each one in turn and ask what it does about that route.

Try it on a white roof, which is the book’s own example. Colour acts on radiation, so the roof absorbs less of the sunlight falling on it. That is the only route the colour touches. The other two are downstream of it. A cooler slab conducts less heat down into the ceiling, and a cooler ceiling warms the air under it less. So naming the route tells you where the control bites, not which routes end up different. Whether the white roof is enough depends on how much of the heat was arriving as sunlight on the roof in the first place.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The heat equation holds only while the substance stays the same substance in the same phase. Boil the water and it stops. The energy then goes into turning liquid into steam, and the temperature sits still while that happens. Any calculation that crosses a boiling point or a melting point has left this section behind.

Specific heat is not truly a constant. Over the ranges used here the variation is small enough to ignore.

A person is not one substance and has no single specific heat you can look up. Nothing here gives you a figure for heating or cooling a person, and none of these numbers should be carried across to one.

All three routes run at once in every real situation. Naming the route a control acts on does not settle what the other two then do.

This section gives no rates. It says by which routes heat moves and never how fast.

Sweating is not one of the three, and the book does not treat it as one. Any claim that turns on evaporation is outside what you are holding.

“Only three methods” is a claim about routes across a boundary. It is not a promise that every warming or cooling you meet is explained by naming one. A person getting warmer may be doing it by running a chemical reaction inside their own boundary. That is not a transfer across the boundary at all.

points.html: A bigger temperature rise does not mean more heat went in. Give a kilogram of steel and a kilogram of water the same energy. The steel rises more than nine times as far. So a thermometer reading is not an energy.
Heat is energy on the way, not a thing an object holds, so refuse the sentence “this object contains so much heat”. Heat is the name of a transfer.

When anyone turns a temperature reading into an energy, ask two things. What heat capacity did they use? Where did it come from? Inside one machine the heat capacity is fixed, so the reading can be trusted. Across two machines a degree is not a degree. Rises set side by side with no heat capacity named are not energies set side by side.
Water needs more than nine times the energy that iron or steel needs, for the same rise in the same mass. The figures are 4186 joules per kilogram per degree Celsius at 15.0 °C, against 452.

The heat equation holds only while the substance stays the same substance in the same phase. It breaks at every boiling point, every melting point and every chemical reaction. When a calculation reaches one of those points, stop rather than substitute.
A temperature is not an amount of energy, so never read a patient’s temperature as a statement about energy gained or lost. One is in degrees and the other in joules.

Heat moves by conduction, convection and radiation, and by nothing else, so make every claim about keeping warm or cool name its route. Once the route is named, the question becomes how much was arriving that way, and that can be answered.
Teach the two-objects demonstration before the formula. After that they will not read a rise as an energy again.

blocks.prompt:
Without looking back, write down the difference between heat and temperature, with the unit of each.

Then name the three ways heat moves, and give one example of each from a kitchen.
blocks.answer:
Heat is the transfer of energy from a hotter thing to a colder thing, and it happens because the two are at different temperatures. It is an amount of energy and its unit is the joule.

Temperature is how hot something is. It is a level rather than an amount, and its unit is the degree Celsius or the kelvin.

The test that separates them: temperature does not care how much of the thing there is, and heat does. A spoonful and a bucket of boiling water are at the same temperature and hold very different amounts of energy.

The three ways heat moves.

Conduction is transfer through matter that is staying put, by contact. A steel tumbler of hot chai warming your fingers.

Convection is transfer by a fluid moving and taking the energy with it. The hot air rising off a tawa onto your palm held above it.

Radiation is transfer as electromagnetic radiation, emitted or absorbed, with nothing needed in between. The warmth on your face from an open tandoor across the room.

One thing to check in your own answer. Did you write a unit for each of the first two? If heat and temperature came out with the same unit, or with no unit, the distinction has not been made yet.

blocks.prompt:
A sheet for a “heat-retaining” food container says this.

The double steel wall keeps food hot for six hours, so no energy escapes and the food keeps all its calories.

The container and the sheet are made up for this exercise. Say what is wrong, and say what you would ask for.
blocks.answer:
There are three claims stacked here and they get weaker as you go along.

The first claim is about a rate. A double wall slows conduction, because the gap between the two walls has less matter in it to conduct through. It slows convection too, if the air in the gap cannot circulate. That is a real mechanism and it is checkable. Note that it says nothing about radiation, which is the third route and crosses a gap perfectly well.

The second claim does not follow from the first. “Keeps food hot for six hours” is a statement about how fast energy leaves. “No energy escapes” is a statement that none does. Those are different claims, and only the weaker one can be true. If the food is still hotter than the room after six hours, energy is still crossing. Energy crosses whenever there is a temperature difference. What the container has done is make the crossing slow, not stop it.

The third claim is a change of subject. Calories in food are chemical energy sitting in the food’s molecules. The energy leaving a hot container is thermal energy, and it is leaving because the food is hotter than the room. Letting the food go cold does not remove the chemical energy from it, and keeping it hot does not add any. A cold roti and a hot roti hold the same chemical energy. The sheet has run two different energies together under one word.

What to ask for. First, the rate: how many degrees does the food fall in six hours, starting from what temperature, in a room at what temperature. That is the only measurable version of the first claim. Second, which of the three routes the wall acts on, and what it does about radiation. Third, nothing at all for the third claim, because it should be withdrawn rather than supported.

blocks.prompt:
A first-year resident has ten minutes and a whiteboard. They have used a calorimeter and they are confident that a bigger temperature rise means more energy.

Teach them why that is true inside one instrument and false between two, so that they leave able to challenge a temperature-based energy claim.
blocks.answer:
Ten minutes, a whiteboard, and somebody who is not wrong yet — they are right about the instrument and about to over-apply it.

Start by agreeing with them, out loud, and write the calorimeter sentence on the board. Twice the rise, twice the energy. Tell them it is correct and you are not going to take it away.

Then draw two circles and label them: one kilogram of water, one kilogram of steel. Ask the room how far each goes up if you put the same energy into both. Let them answer before you write anything; most will say the same amount.

Now write the two numbers from the table. Water 4186 joules per kilogram per degree. Steel 452. Then bracket the steel’s rise on the board, so they watch it happen rather than watch a calculator.

452 times 9 = 4068
452 times 10 = 4520

Four thousand one hundred and eighty-six joules sits between those two. So the tawa goes up by between nine and ten degrees, while the water goes up by one. Same energy, one goes up nine times as far. That is the moment to stop and say nothing for a few seconds. The sentence they walked in with has just broken in front of them.

Now rebuild it, and this is the part they will keep. Write the equation, naming every letter as you write it. Q is the quantity of heat. m is the mass. c is the specific heat of the material. ΔT is the change in temperature. Then point at c and say that this is the thing that was hiding.

Inside one calorimeter, m and c never change from run to run. So the rise is the energy divided by a number that never moves, and their original sentence is exactly right. Give that number its name on the board: the heat capacity of the instrument, joules per degree.

Change the instrument and the number changes. Change the object and the number changes. Then degrees from one are not degrees from the other, and a comparison of rises is not a comparison of energies.

Close with the question you want them asking on Monday. When anybody reports an energy that came from a temperature, ask what heat capacity was used and where it came from. Tell them that “we used the calorimeter’s energy equivalent” is a good answer. “We compared the temperature rises” is not an answer at all.

blocks.prompt: Work out the value of m times c times ΔT when m is 2, c is 500 and ΔT is 30.
blocks.answer:
Put the three numbers in place of the three letters and multiply.

2 times 500 times 30 = 30000

Thirty thousand.

Take the multiplication in two steps if that is easier, and check you get the same.

2 times 500 = 1000
1000 times 30 = 30000

blocks.prompt:
Two parts, both on the same relationship.

  1. Q is 30,000, m is 2 and c is 500. Work out ΔT.

  2. Q is 9,000, m is 3 and ΔT is 6. Work out c.
blocks.answer:
Both parts run the same relationship backwards. Q is the product of the other three, so any one of them is Q divided by the product of the two you have.

a) Multiply the two you have.

2 times 500 = 1000

Then divide.

30000 divided by 1000 = 30

ΔT is 30.

b) Same move, with a different letter missing.

3 times 6 = 18
9000 divided by 18 = 500

c is 500.

Check each one forwards before you leave it.

2 times 500 times 30 = 30000
3 times 500 times 6 = 9000

blocks.prompt:
A steel degchi weighing 1.2 kilograms holds 2 kilograms of water. Both are heated from 28 degrees Celsius to 100 degrees Celsius.

Take the specific heat of water as 4186 joules per kilogram per degree Celsius. Take that of steel as 452.

Work out the energy that went into the water, the energy that went into the steel, and the total. Keep the unit on every answer. Then say which of the two took more, and why.
blocks.answer:
First the change in temperature, which is the same for both.

100 minus 28 = 72

Seventy-two degrees Celsius.

Now the water. Mass times specific heat first.

2 times 4186 = 8372

Eight thousand three hundred and seventy-two joules for every degree. Now times the 72 degrees.

8372 times 72 = 602784

Six hundred and two thousand seven hundred and eighty-four joules into the water.

Now the steel, the same way.

1.2 times 452 = 542.4
542.4 times 72 = 39052.8

Thirty-nine thousand and fifty-two point eight joules into the steel.

The total.

602784 plus 39052.8 = 641836.8

Six hundred and forty-one thousand eight hundred and thirty-six point eight joules altogether.

Which took more, and why. The water, by a long way — about fifteen times as much. Two reasons stack. There is more of it, 2 kilograms against 1.2. And water needs more than nine times as many joules per kilogram per degree as steel does. The vessel is almost an afterthought in the arithmetic. That is why a pan of water takes so long to heat, and the empty pan takes almost no time at all.

blocks.prompt:
A glass tumbler weighing 0.18 kilograms and a steel tumbler weighing 0.18 kilograms are each filled with hot chai. Each tumbler itself rises by 55 degrees Celsius.

Take the specific heat of glass as 840 joules per kilogram per degree Celsius. Take that of iron and steel as 452.

Work out how much energy each tumbler absorbed, with its unit. Then say which tumbler takes more energy out of the chai, and what that means for the chai in each.
blocks.answer:
The glass first. Mass times specific heat.

0.18 times 840 = 151.2

A hundred and fifty-one point two joules for each degree. Now times 55 degrees.

151.2 times 55 = 8316

Eight thousand three hundred and sixteen joules into the glass tumbler.

Now the steel.

0.18 times 452 = 81.36
81.36 times 55 = 4474.8

Four thousand four hundred and seventy-four point eight joules into the steel tumbler.

Which takes more. The glass. Now put a size on how many times more, and bracket it rather than divide. Try 1.8 times the steel’s figure.

4474.8 times 1.8 = 8054.64

Eight thousand and fifty-four, and the glass took 8,316. So the factor is more than 1.8. Now try 1.9.

4474.8 times 1.9 = 8502.12

Eight thousand five hundred and two, which is more than the glass took. So the factor sits between 1.8 and 1.9. A calculator puts it at 1.858.

Now check that against the two specific heats, by multiplying 452 by the same figure and seeing whether 840 comes back.

452 times 1.858 = 839.816

Eight hundred and thirty-nine point eight, which is 840 to the nearest whole number. The ratio of the energies is the ratio of the specific heats. It has to be. The two tumblers have the same mass and the same temperature change, and differ only in the material.

What it means for the chai. Every joule that goes into warming the tumbler came out of the chai. So the glass tumbler takes about 1.86 times as much energy out of it. With the same amount of chai poured into each, the two tumblers could not both rise the full 55 degrees. The glass would stop lower, and so would the chai in it.

And one thing this does not settle. How fast the chai then goes on cooling depends on the routes out of the tumbler. How well each material conducts, how thick the wall is, how much surface meets the air. This calculation is about the energy taken up in warming the vessel, and it is only the first part of the story.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke.

500 grams of water is heated from 30 degrees Celsius to 80 degrees Celsius
the specific heat of water is 4186 joules per kilogram per degree Celsius
80 minus 30 = 50
500 times 4186 times 50 = 104650000
so the water absorbed 104,650,000 joules
blocks.answer:
The step that broke is the fourth, and the arithmetic in it is correct. What broke is a unit.

The specific heat is quoted per kilogram. The mass was put in as grams. Multiplying grams by a per-kilogram figure gives an answer a thousand times too big. Nothing on the page says so, because the units were never written beside the numbers.

Convert the mass first.

500 divided by 1000 = 0.5

Half a kilogram. Now the same calculation with the mass in the unit the specific heat is quoted in.

0.5 times 4186 times 50 = 104650

A hundred and four thousand six hundred and fifty joules, which is about 105 kilojoules.

A size check would have caught it. The two answers are a thousand times apart, which is the kind of gap the section on orders of magnitude exists to make visible.

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable. Every number in it is a real number. The subtraction is right and the multiplication is right. The specific heat is the correct one for water. The only thing wrong is that two of the quantities were measured in units that do not go together. That never shows up in the digits.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke.

a 1 kilogram steel tawa and 1 kilogram of water start at 30.0 degrees Celsius
each is put on an identical burner for the same length of time
after that time the tawa reads 39.3 degrees Celsius and the water reads 31.0
the tawa’s temperature rose by much more than the water’s
so much more heat went into the tawa than into the water
blocks.answer:
The step that broke is the last one. The two temperature rises are very different and the two quantities of heat are almost the same.

Work out each one, using the specific heats from the table: water 4186 joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, steel 452.

The tawa first.

39.3 minus 30.0 = 9.3
1 times 452 times 9.3 = 4203.6

About 4,204 joules.

Now the water.

31.0 minus 30.0 = 1.0
1 times 4186 times 1.0 = 4186

About 4,186 joules.

Put the two side by side.

4203.6 minus 4186 = 17.6

Seventeen point six joules apart, out of roughly four thousand two hundred each. That is well under one per cent, which is smaller than the error in reading either thermometer. The two burners delivered the same energy, which is what the second line of the working said they did.

What the fourth line should have led to instead. A temperature rise is the heat divided by the object’s mass times its specific heat. The two objects have the same mass and very different specific heats, so the same heat has to produce very different rises. The rises differ because the objects differ, not because the energies differ.

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable. Lines one to four are all correct, and the last line is the sentence anybody carries away from using a calorimeter, where it is true. The missing step is the one that asks whether the two things being compared need the same energy per degree. Inside a single instrument that question never has to be asked.

blocks.prompt:
A poster in a gym says this.

Drink four litres of chilled water a day, straight from the fridge at 5 degrees. Your body has to warm every litre up to 37 degrees, and that is energy spent without moving a muscle.

The poster and both temperatures are made up for this problem. Take the four litres as four kilograms of water.

Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what your answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
What to compute: the energy needed to warm four kilograms of water through the temperature range the poster names. The prompt gives the mass as four kilograms. That figure is the only quantity the poster’s claim actually pins down, and it is worth knowing before arguing about anything else.

The change in temperature first.

37 minus 5 = 32

Thirty-two degrees Celsius. Now the mass times the specific heat of water.

4 times 4186 = 16744

Then times the change.

16744 times 32 = 535808

Five hundred and thirty-five thousand eight hundred and eight joules, which is about 536 kilojoules. Now put it in the unit food labels use. One kilocalorie is 4,184 joules, from the section on energy units.

That 4,184 is the calorie’s definition, not water’s specific heat. The two are different quantities.

So ask how many kilocalories fit in 535,808 joules. Try 128.

4184 times 128 = 535552

Five hundred and thirty-five thousand five hundred and fifty-two, which is just short of what you have.

535808 minus 535552 = 256

Two hundred and fifty-six joules short, which is well under one kilocalorie. So the answer is a shade over 128 kilocalories a day, if every part of the poster’s set-up holds.

What this does not establish, and there are four things.

It does not establish that the body spends that energy on top of what it was already spending. The balance from the section on conservation and the boundary says the numbers must add up across that boundary. It says nothing about whether the other crossings stay put when you change one of them. Whether they do is a question about bodies, and it is the subject of the booklet on energy balance rather than of this section.

It does not establish anything about body weight. The answer is in kilojoules. Weight is in kilograms. Nothing here converts one into the other.

It does not establish the two temperatures. They are the poster’s, and they were taken as given so that the arithmetic could be done. A different pair gives a different answer in proportion.

And it does not establish that all four litres arrive at 5 degrees and are warmed through the full 32 degrees inside the person. Water sitting in a glass in an Indian kitchen does not stay at fridge temperature for long.

What is left after all that is a number: 128 kilocalories a day. It is a ceiling on the size of the effect the poster describes, not a measurement of it. That is still worth having, because it stops the claim being either dismissed or believed without a figure.

blocks.prompt:
Someone says this in a meeting about food testing.

The bomb in our calorimeter has a heat capacity of 893 joules per degree Celsius. We ran two foods. One gave a rise of 4.2 degrees and the other 2.1 degrees. So the first food holds twice the energy of the second.

Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what your answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
What to compute: the energy behind each rise, using the bomb’s own heat capacity, and then the ratio of the two. The heat capacity is in joules per degree, so multiply it by the degrees. Note what that figure is and is not. It is the bomb, not the whole calorimeter.

The first food.

893 times 4.2 = 3750.6

About 3,751 joules absorbed by the bomb.

The second.

893 times 2.1 = 1875.3

About 1,875 joules.

Now the ratio.

3750.6 divided by 1875.3 = 2

Exactly two, which it was always going to be, because the same heat capacity multiplies both rises. On the conditions stated, the colleague’s arithmetic is right.

What this does not establish, and the conditions are where all of it sits.

It does not establish anything if the two runs were not done in the same calorimeter. A degree is worth 893 joules in this bomb and some other figure in another one. So rises from two instruments cannot be compared at all until both heat capacities are in hand.

It does not establish that one food holds twice the energy of the other unless the two samples weighed the same. Energy content is quoted per gram. Burn twice as much of an identical food and you get twice the rise, and nothing about the food has changed.

It does not account for everything that absorbed the energy. The 893 joules per degree is the bomb itself. A bomb calorimeter sits in water, and the water takes up energy too. So the total released by the food is larger than either figure computed here.

And it does not establish what reaches a person. The boundary round the bomb is not the boundary round a body, and what crosses the two is not the same quantity.

What to say in the meeting. The ratio is sound and it is a ratio of temperature rises in one instrument. Before it becomes a statement about two foods, someone has to confirm three things. The same calorimeter, the same sample mass, and the water as well as the bomb.
